title: Essential Skills Assessment Series & Diagnostic Engine

contributors.contribution: Co-designed the MVC/Swing architecture with Jamie, reviewed architectural decisions, and mentored Jamie in MVC, Swing architecture, MVP thinking, and practical software-design discipline.
Worked with Jamie to design the educational assessment logic, diagnostic categories, placement rules, and literacy-testing content.

description: I helped design and built the Essential Skills Assessment Series, a Java/Swing literacy assessment platform that did more than score answers: it analyzed student errors by underlying reading, phonics, decoding, and spelling concepts and used the results to guide teachers toward appropriate instructional programs and units. This was my first major architecture/design project, my first experiment with an ISAM content database, and the beginning of a long mentorship with a former Sun Microsystems consultant who helped me develop the MVC architecture and mature my software-design approach.

sections.title: Assessment Series
paragraphs: The Essential Skills Assessment Series was a family of literacy assessment products designed to measure student performance and diagnose specific reading, spelling, phonics, and decoding weaknesses.
The system combined student-facing testing with a teacher-facing Assessment Manager for assigning tests, managing students, configuring assessments, and reviewing results.

sections.title: Six Production Assessments
paragraphs: Surviving Essential Skills installation material identifies six assessment products in the series.

sections.title: Assessment Manager & Student Assignments
paragraphs: Teachers used the Assessment Manager to create classes and student accounts, configure and assign tests, and review assessment results.
Students completed assigned tests through the separate Student Assignments application.

sections.title: Diagnostic Error Analysis
paragraphs: The diagnostic tests were designed to determine why a student answered incorrectly rather than only recording a final score.

For spelling, different incorrect responses to the same word could expose different underlying misconceptions. For example, variations of a word such as 'cave' could indicate different weaknesses in phonics, vowel patterns, or spelling conventions.

sections.title: Teacher-Designed Diagnostic Logic
paragraphs: I worked closely with two teachers, including the company's vice president, to design the diagnostic logic.
The teachers brought the literacy and curriculum expertise while I helped translate those educational concepts into rules, data structures, scoring logic, and software behavior.

sections.title: Concept-Level Assessment
paragraphs: Diagnostic reports grouped performance around underlying concepts rather than treating every incorrect answer as equivalent.
This allowed the system to isolate areas such as phonics patterns, vowel sounds, consonant behavior, decoding skills, and spelling concepts.

sections.title: Diagnostic Phonics
paragraphs: The Diagnostic Phonics Test evaluated multiple foundational phonics concepts and exposed weaknesses that could then be addressed through corresponding Essential Skills instructional material.

sections.title: Diagnostic Spelling Skills
paragraphs: The Diagnostic Spelling Skills Test analyzed spelling performance at the component-skill level.
Individual words could test more than one diagnostic area, allowing a relatively compact assessment to reveal multiple types of weakness.

sections.title: Diagnostic Decoding Skills
paragraphs: The Diagnostic Decoding Skills Test used auditory and nonsense-word style exercises to determine whether students could apply phonics rules rather than relying only on memorized vocabulary.
Results could expose weaknesses in consonants, vowels, blends, digraphs, diphthongs, and related decoding concepts.

sections.title: Graded Assessments
paragraphs: The graded assessments measured broader student placement and performance rather than only diagnostic subskills.
Reading, spelling, and word-recognition results could be used to estimate instructional level and help teachers select appropriate Essential Skills programs.

sections.title: Placement Into Instruction
paragraphs: Assessment results were intended to lead directly into instruction.
Reports could guide teachers toward the Essential Skills programs or units that addressed the weaknesses identified by the assessment rather than leaving the teacher with an isolated score.

sections.title: Mastery & Instructional Levels
paragraphs: Assessment reporting classified performance into instructional categories such as mastery, independent, instructional, and frustration levels.
This gave teachers a more useful interpretation of the raw score and supported placement decisions.

sections.title: Configurable Testing
paragraphs: Teachers could configure how assessments were administered rather than using a single rigid test mode.
items: Stopping after a configurable number of consecutive incorrect answers
Selecting specific test units or components

sections.title: Teacher Reports
paragraphs: The Assessment Manager provided multiple ways to inspect student results.

sections.title: Answer-Level Review
paragraphs: The Answers report showed the individual test questions and the student's responses so teachers could inspect exactly where errors occurred rather than relying only on aggregate scores.

sections.title: My First Major Architecture Project
paragraphs: This project marked one of my first major shifts from primarily implementing software into actively designing the architecture.
I was responsible for shaping the system while working with an experienced former Sun Microsystems consultant who reviewed my decisions and helped guide me toward cleaner architectural solutions.

sections.title: Learning MVC
paragraphs: The consultant introduced me to Model-View-Controller architecture, which had not been covered in my college program.
We designed the Swing/MVC architecture together, with me doing the architectural and implementation work while he reviewed, challenged, and refined the design.

sections.title: Engineering Mentorship
paragraphs: The collaboration also introduced me to practical engineering ideas such as Minimum Viable Product, avoiding unnecessary 'kitchen sink' features, and separating essential architecture from premature polish.
Although I already knew Swing, the project substantially deepened my understanding of building larger Swing applications cleanly.

sections.title: First ISAM Experiment
paragraphs: The Assessment Series was my first experiment with using an ISAM-style database for application content.
At this stage, student marks were still persisted using serialized Java classes rather than the more mature database architecture that followed.

sections.title: Database Architecture Evolution
paragraphs: The Assessment Series predates the later SE / Version 2 database redesign.
The database ideas explored here became part of the evolution toward the more mature networkable ISAM B-tree architecture used in subsequent Essential Skills systems.

sections.title: Network Deployment
paragraphs: The Assessment Series was designed for real school deployment and supported shared server installations where student data could be accessed across client workstations.
That deployment model fit the wider Essential Skills environment of teacher/admin workstations, student computers, and shared school-server storage.

sections.title: Long-Term Architecture Influence
paragraphs: The assessment project influenced later Essential Skills work well beyond the original tests.
Its diagnostic and placement ideas, database evolution, reporting concepts, teacher workflows, and architecture mentorship fed into later SE, Teacher Management, Hydra-Gen, and pre/post-test systems.

The consultant later retired fully and is deceased; do not use those personal details publicly.

Surviving Essential Skills installation material identifies six assessment products: Graded Reading Comprehension Test, Graded Spelling Test, Graded Word Recognition Test, Diagnostic Phonics Test, Diagnostic Spelling Skills Test, and Diagnostic Decoding Skills Test.
The teacher-facing application was called Assessment Manager.
The student-facing testing application was called Student Assignments.
Assessment reporting included Completed Assignments, Scores, Answers, and Graph views.
The assessments could use configurable time limits, stopping rules based on consecutive incorrect answers, and selected test units/components.
Diagnostic results were organized around underlying concepts, while graded assessments supported broader placement decisions.
Assessment results could guide teachers toward relevant Essential Skills programs/units.
Surviving installation documentation confirms server-based deployment with shared student data across client workstations.
